Adiposity and Cardiometabolic Risk in Children With
and Without Antipsychotic Drug Treatment
Ginger E. Nicol,MD1, Lisa de las Fuentes,MD,2, Amy E. Riek,MD,3,
Carlos Bernal-Mizrachi,MD,3, Eric J. Lenze,MD1, J. Phillip Miller,AB4,
Julia A. Schweiger,CCRC1, Michael D. Yingling,MS1, Vincent J. Huang,BA1,
David J. Dixon,PhD1, Charles H. Hennekens,MD,5, John W. Newcomer,MD6
1Healthy Mind Lab, Department of Psychiatry, WA University School of Medicine in St. Louis, MO;
2Department of Internal Medicine, Division of Cardiology, Division of Biostatistics, WA University School
of Medicine in St. Louis, MO; 3Department of Internal Medicine, Division of Endocrinology, Metabolism
and Lipid Research, WA University School of Medicine in St. Louis, MO; 4Division of Biostatistics, WA
University School of Medicine in St. Louis, MO; 5Integrated Medical Science Department, First Sir Richard
Doll Professor, Charles E. Schmidt College of Medicine, FL Atlantic University, Boca Raton, FL;
6Department of Clinical Biomedical Science, Charles E. Schmidt College of Medicine, FL Atlantic
University, Boca Raton, FL
Context: Pediatric obesity is common, particularly in children treated with antipsychotic medica-
tions. Antipsychotic exposure can increase cardiometabolic risk by increasing adiposity, and pos-
sibly via other adiposity-independent pathways.
Objective: To characterize relationships of adiposity with intra-hepatic triglyceride content (IHTG)
and carotid intima media thickness (CIMT) in children with and without antipsychotic drug treat-
ment, and explore whether vitamin D alters any effects in these relationships.
Design: Cross sectional case-control study.
Setting: Academic Medical Center.
Patients or other Participants: Participants were 44 children (ages 6–19); 25 cases treated with
antipsychotic and other psychotropic drug therapies and 19 untreated controls, frequency-
matched on age, gender and body mass index.
Main Outcome Measures: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry percent body fat (DEXA %fat), IHTG
measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and CIMT measured by ultrasonography.
Fasting blood glucose, insulin, lipids C-reactive protein, and liver enzymes were also evaluated.
Results: There were no significant differences between cases and controls on measures of IHTG,
CIMT or DEXA %fat. In combined crude and adjusted analyses, DEXA %fat predicted IHTG (R2 
0.30) but not CIMT. Low levels of vitamin D were associated with larger effects of DEXA %fat on
IHTG.
Conclusion: In treated and untreated children alike, adiposity is a significant predictor of liver fat
content. This relationship was altered by low vitamin D level. These results suggest a modifiable
pathway to hepatic steatosis. Further research is needed to test the hypothesis that children with
high adiposity and low Vitamin D have particularly increased risks for the development of fatty
liver.

O
besity is a major independent risk factor for cardio-
vascular disease (CVD) (1) and is rapidly overtak-
ing cigarette smoking as the leading avoidable cause of
death in the United States (US) and other developed as well
as developing countries (2). The prevalence of childhood
obesity is also rising at an alarming rate worldwide, and
obesity-related conditions, such as type 2 diabetes and
fatty liver disease are now emerging in children whereas
they had been seen only in adulthood decades earlier (3).
Children with severe mental illness treated with antipsy-
chotic drugs, perhaps even more than their adult counter-
parts, are at markedly increased risk for developing obe-
sity (4). Such children are at increased risk for the early
development of adverse health conditions such as hyper-
tension, dyslipidemia and insulin resistance leading to
type 2 diabetes (4–8). In addition, antipsychotic drug
treatment may increase cardiometabolic risk independent
of treatment-induced increases in adiposity (8–10).
In adult populations, adiposity is positively correlated
with intra-hepatic triglyceride content (IHTG) (11, 12)
and carotid intima media thickness (CIMT), (13) two
early indices of cardiometabolic risk. Increasing IHTG is
associated with insulin resistance in liver, muscle and ad-
ipose tissue; alterations in free fatty acid metabolism; and
increased
very
low-density
lipoprotein
cholesterol
(LDL-C) and triglyceride secretion rates (12). CIMT is a
quantitative measure of atherosclerosis whose addition to
the Framingham Risk Score improved the prediction of
10-year risk of a first coronary heart disease (CHD) event
in adults having a first myocardial infarction (MI) or
stroke (14).
Low vitamin D (25-hydoxyvitamin D) level ( 30 ng/
ml) (15) is associated with inflammation and cardiovas-
cular disease, and plays a role in complex disease processes
including atherosclerosis and hepatic steatosis (16, 17). In
animal models, the development of nonalcoholic steato-
hepatitis is accelerated by the combination of vitamin D
deficiency and a high fat diet, and reversed by the admin-
istration of 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D3 (18, 19). Further, vi-
tamin D levels have been observed to be low during anti-
psychotic drug treatment (20).
While fatty liver disease and atherosclerosis can begin
in childhood, (21) data regarding the association between
whole body adiposity and either IHTG or CIMT in chil-
dren are sparse (22, 23). Further, there are no published
data on either measure in youth treated with antipsychotic
medications. In this analytic case control study, we tested
the hypothesis that adiposity is associated with IHTG or
CIMT in children with and without antipsychotic and
concomitant psychotropic drug therapies, spanning a
range of adiposity. We also tested whether adiposity is
related to IHTG or CIMT differently in children with and
without psychotropic medication exposure. Since antipsy-
chotic drug exposure significantly increases adiposity, (8)
we designed this study to include the frequency matching
of youth on BMI percentile with and without antipsy-
chotic exposure within age and gender groupings. We also
explored whether low vitamin D levels modify any effect
of adiposity on IHTG or CIMT.
Materials and Methods
Participants
Participants were 6–19 years of age for whom assent and
written informed consent were obtained from the child and par-
ent(s). Children treated with second generation antipsychotics
were 1) recruited from outpatient child psychiatry clinics in the
St. Louis, MO area, 2) met DSM-IV-TR criteria for one or more
childhood-onset psychiatric disorders (determined by both clin-
ical and semistructured diagnostic interview) and 3) had been
taking a stable dose of a second generation antipsychotic for at
least 1 month prior to participation. The Missouri Assessment of
Genetics Interview for Children, (24) a semistructured diagnos-
tic interview, was used to confirm psychiatric diagnoses. Con-
current treatment with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
(SSRIs) and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
medications (including stimulants, atomoxetine or alpha agonist
agents below a total daily dose of 2 mg/kg methylphenidate
equivalent) was permitted in order to increase generalizability of
results, as a large proportion of antipsychotic treated youth are
commonly treated with SSRI’s, stimulants and other medica-
tions, (25) and an increasingly common use of antipsychotic
medication is in treatment resistant ADHD (26). In the present
study, concomitant psychotropic treatment was permitted to in-
crease generalizability of results. In the group of antipsychotic
treated participants, 17 of the 25 were also receiving another
psychotropic medication. Please refer to online supplemental in-
formation for additional details regarding psychiatric diagnoses
and psychotropic medications. Controls were recruited from
outpatient primary care clinics in the St. Louis, MO area and
included physically healthy participants without psychiatric dis-
orders. Clinical rating scales, including the Achenbach Child
Behavior Checklist (CBCL) (27) and the Aberrant Behavior
Checklist (ABC) (28, 29) were administered to rule out clinically
significant behavioral symptoms. Controls were frequency
matched by age, gender, and BMI percentile (lean  5–50; nor-
mal  51–84; overweight/obese  85). Age and gender specific
BMI percentiles were calculated using the EpiInfo software de-
veloped by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
(30). Race and ethnicity were self-reported by the primary care-
giver. Participants were recruited from the St. Louis metropoli-
tan area, where 2013 US Census Bureau statistics report 46.4%
of the total population are Caucasian, 47.9% are Black or Af-
rican American, 3.1% are Asian, 0.3% are American Indian or
Alaska Native, and 3.7% Hispanic or Latino (31). Groups were
not matched on ethnicity, as there was no hypothesis regarding
differential effects of ethnicity on the metabolic or weight gain
effects of psychotropic drugs. Exclusion criteria for both cases
and controls included medical disorders or treatment for a met-
abolic disorder that could confound the assessment of plasma or
imagingtests;concurrenttreatmentwithsedatingantihistamines

Study Tests and Procedures
Whole body percent fat was measured using Dual Energy
X-Ray
Absorptiometry
(DEXA)
(Delphi
W
densitometer
equipped with version 12.4 software; Hologic, Waltham, MA).
IHTG was determined using proton magnetic resonance spec-
troscopy with a 1.5T scanner (MAGNETOM Sonata; Siemens,
Erlangen, Germany), with all frequencies (ie, chemical shifts)
measured relative to the principal water 1H resonance referenced
at zero. CIMT was measured via 7-MHz B-mode carotid ultra-
sonography (Sequoia C512, Acuson-Siemens, Mountain View,
CA). A single sonographer, masked to case-control status, ac-
quired B-mode images of carotid arteries in the longitudinal axis
bilaterally. A 1 cm region of the common carotid artery proximal
to the bifurcation was identified and exported for offline analysis
with ProSolv software (FUJIFILM Medical Systems USA, Stam-
ford, CT). CIMT measures were obtained by taking the average
of far-wall intima media thickness from both left and right com-
mon carotid arteries. Each site represents the average of three
measures of the maximum CIMT, obtained by two separate
blinded raters. The interobserver intraclass correlation coeffi-
cient was 0.70. Blood pressure was obtained using a right upper
extremity while patients were sitting. Plasma measures of me-
tabolism obtained for all cases and controls included fasting vi-
tamin D (25-hydoxyvitamin D), glucose, insulin, and lipids, as
well as C-reactive protein (CRP) and a liver panel (aspartate
aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), alka-
line phosphatase, total protein, fibrinogen, albumin and
bilirubin).
Data Analysis
To test for the statistical significance of any differences be-
tweencasesandcontrols,weusedt-testsforcontinuousvariables
and Chi-Square tests for categorical variables. Analysis of Vari-
ance (ANOVA) models were used to test the significance of case-
control status on IHTG and CIMT, respectively. No significant
differences between cases and controls for IHTG, CIMT, and
whole-body DEXA %fat were found. Thus, we were able to
explore the interrelationships of whole body DEXA %fat to
IHTG and CIMT by constructing separate analysis of covariance
(ANCOVA) models with IHTG and CIMT as dependent vari-
ables, respectively. Both models included independent variables
for DEXA %fat and case-control status. Finally, the interaction
of DEXA %fat and case-control status was forced in the AN-
COVA models in order to test whether the slopes differed ac-
cording to case-control status. These models were run with and
without additional independent variables for gender, ethnicity
and age. To test whether low vitamin D level altered the rela-
tionships between DEXA %fat with IHTG and CIMT, respec-
tively, ANCOVA models were rerun with vitamin D level, de-
termined low vs high based on a median split of the obtained
values (19.6 ng/mL, range 8.83–38.73), was added to the model
as an additional independent variable (covariate). All analyses
were performed using SPSS software, V22.
Results
Participant Characteristics
Of 44 participants, 25 were cases and 19 were controls.
Table 1 provides baseline characteristics of the sample,
including a description of anthropomorphic measures and
variousserologicmarkersofmetabolicrisk.Therewereno
significant differences between antipsychotic treated cases
and nonantipsychotic treated controls for DEXA %fat,
CIMT, IHTG or other markers of metabolic risk. All vari-
ables (Table 1) were normally distributed, with the excep-
tion of IHTG, BMI percentile, fasting insulin, high sensi-
tivity CRP (hs-CRP), total bilirubin, and fibrinogen.
Whole Body Adiposity, IHTG and CIMT
Whole body adiposity, measured by DEXA %fat, was
significantly associated with IHTG with no differences
observed by case-control status (Figure 1). In the initial
ANOVA models testing the effect of case-control status on
IHTG and CIMT respectively, no main effect of case-con-
trol status was observed on IHTG (F(1, 42)  1.46, P 
.23) or CIMT (F(1, 42)  0.55, P  .46). In the ANCOVA
model where IHTG served as the dependent variable with
case-control status and DEXA %fat as independent vari-
ables, there was a significant main effect of DEXA %fat on
IHTG (F(1, 42)  16.26, P  .0001) with no significant
main effect of case-control status (F(1, 42)  0.79, P 
.38),consistentwiththeobservedeffectofadiposityonthe
risk of hepatic steatosis in adults. The R2 for this model
was 0.31. There was no interaction between DEXA %fat
and case-control status (F(1, 42)  1.42, P  .24). The
distribution of IHTG values was skewed to higher values.
This curvilinear relationship between DEXA %fat and
IHTG was explored in two ways: 1) IHTG was log-trans-
formed (F(1, 42)  19.29, P  .0001, R2  0.33); 2) Two
potential outliers in the antipsychotic treated group were
excluded (F(1, 40)  15.97, P  .0001, R2  0.30). Both
approaches explained similar overall variance. In this
study sample, DEXA %fat was not associated with CIMT
(Figure 2). In an ANCOVA model where CIMT served as
the dependent variable with case-control status and
DEXA total % fat as the independents, there was no sig-
nificant main effect of DEXA %fat on CIMT (F(1, 42) 
0.07, P  .80), and no main effect of case-control status
(F(1, 42)  0.49, P  .49). The lack of significant inter-
action between DEXA %fat and case-control status sat-
isfies the ANCOVA assumption of homogeneity of regres-
sion slopes (F(1, 42)  0.15, P  .70). Introducing age,
gender and ethnicity into the primary ANCOVA models
did not alter the significance of any effects (ethnicity was
coded as white vs nonwhite due to small numbers of
Asians (n  1) and Hispanics (n  1)).
Finally, we tested the effect of BMI percentile instead of

mation for BMI and a log transformation for IHTG, and
the significant association between BMI percentile and
IHTG persisted (F(1, 42)  7.86, P  .01).
Low Vitamin D Level and IHTG
Vitamin D levels altered the relationship between
DEXA %fat and IHTG content, with the strongest rela-
tionship association between DEXA %fat and IHTG oc-
curring in the presence of lower vitamin D level. In the
ANCOVA model where IHTG served as the dependent
variable, including case-control status and both DEXA
%fat and vitamin D level as covariates, there was a sig-
nificant interaction between DEXA %fat and vitamin D
(F(1, 42)  6.83, P  .013). To demonstrate the direc-
tionality of this interaction, we used the primary AN-
COVA model (ie, IHTG as the dependent variable, and
DEXA %fat as well as case-control status as independent
variables) with median split low vs high vitamin D levels.
The significant relationship between DEXA %fat and
IHTG was associated with lower (F(1, 20)  11.67, P 
.003) but not higher (F(1, 21)  0.27, P  .61) vitamin D
levels (see Figures 3a and b). Rerunning this same AN-
COVA with the low Vitamin D cohort redefined as either
as 20 ng/mL [deficiency] or 30 ng.mL [insufficiency]
rather than the lower half of the median split, similarly
resulted in a significant relationship between DEXA %fat
and IHTG (Deficiency: F(1, 22)9.74, P  .006; Insuffi-
ciency: F(1, 38)13.73, P  .001). To further explore the
effect of vitamin D we tested for nonspecific effects of
inflammation as an additional modifier of DEXA %fat
effects on IHTG. Specifically, we added CRP as an addi-
tional independent variable in the model that included
DEXA %fat and vitamin D level as independent variables
predicting IHTG. The introduction of hs-CRP into the
model did not alter the significance
of either main effect of DEXA %fat
on IHTG ((F(1, 41)  9.08, P 
.005) or the interaction of DEXA
%fat and vitamin D on IHTG (F(1,
41)  4.83, P  .034). Vitamin D
level did not alter the lack of a sig-
nificant relationship between DEXA
%fat and CIMT, with no interaction
between DEXA %fat and vitamin D
level (F(1, 42)  1.44, P  .24) and
no main effect of DEXA %fat (F(1,
42)  1.71, P  .20) or Vitamin D
level (F(1, 42)  2.54, P  .12) on
CIMT. As noted previously, the dis-
tribution

was

mations for the skewed variables IHTG and hsCRP. Fi-
nally, the effect of age on Vitamin D levels was explored,
treating age as a continuous variable (F(1, 43)1.21, P 
.28), and looking at younger vs older children using the

Discussion
These data show at least three key observations. First, we
observed a significant association between DEXA-mea-
sured whole body adiposity and IHTG in children, as has
been previously reported (32). We did not observe a sig-
nificant association between adiposity and CIMT. Sec-
ond, the statistical relationship between whole body adi-
posity and IHTG was not affected by psychotropic drug
treatment status, suggesting the primary clinical impor-
tance of the overall level of adiposity achieved indepen-
dent of cause. Third, in an exploratory analysis, the
strength of the relationship between body fat and IHTG
appeared to be altered by vitamin D level. Specifically,
among those with lower vitamin D level, the observed
association between whole body adiposity and IHTG was
larger and more significant. This report, to our knowl-
edge, offers the first results in children regarding biomark-
ers relevant to whole body adiposity, IHTG, and CIMT,
key indicators of cardiometabolic risk. These results sug-
gest pathways to hepatosteatosis in children that may be
modifiable by screening for and treatment of excess adi-
posity and low vitamin D levels.
This study was designed to provide minimal differences
in BMI between treated cases and untreated controls.
Studies evaluating metabolic risk during antipsychotic
treatment in children have generally observed significant

untreated youth, (4) as well as in untreated general pop-
ulation controls (5, 6). The observation that matching on
BMI percentile attenuates these previously observed dif-
ferences between treated and untreated children on a va-
riety of metabolic outcomes further underscores the im-
portant role of adiposity in contributing to metabolic risk.
Thus, the current results suggest that the level of adiposity
achieved, independent of whether this is related to psy-
chotropic treatment or not, is the major determinant of
hepatic triglyceride content. The current observations are
important, because in children as well as adults, increased
hepaticfatisassociatedwithinsulinresistance,andmaybe
a more accurate and earlier risk indicator than circulating
triglyceride levels (33) or the presence of visceral abdom-
inal fat (12). IHTG correlates well with liver biopsy re-
sults, is associated with metabolic risk in children, (34)
and is an indicator of response to weight loss treatment in
youth (35).
We did not find an association between adiposity and
CIMT. Possible explanations for the lack of association
between adiposity and CIMT in this study could be related
to the relatively small sample size. Additionally, CIMT
represents a structural result of increased inflammation
and plaque buildup that develops over time, and high lev-
els of adiposity achieved in youth have been correlated
with CIMT in adulthood (37). Since inflammation and
plaque development are pathophysiological changes as-
sociatedwithchronicobesity,CIMTmaybeamoredown-
stream indicator of metabolic risk than adiposity or he-
patic steatosis. The cross sectional nature of the present
study, as well as the age of the population thus offer plau-
sible explanations for the lack of association found in the
current data. This latter possibility is supported by our
observation that CIMT levels in all study participants fell
within normal pediatric ranges observed in previous work
(38).
Vitamin D level has been implicated in the development
of complex disease processes associated with cardiometa-
bolic risk, and supplementation improves metabolic pa-
rameters (39). There is little evidence, however, to support
current screening and treatment practices in general (40).
Vitamin D levels are low during antipsychotic drug treat-
ment, (20) with supplementation proposed as a strategy to
reduce metabolic side effects and weight gain. For exam-
ple, in an inpatient cohort of antipsychotic treated youth
(n  136), most individuals had very low vitamin D level
(15ng/ml), regardless of diagnosis or type of antipsy-
chotic treatment (20). Further, the evidence supporting
treatment of low vitamin D level has been equivocal. In a
small 8 week pilot and feasibility study in inpatient ado-
lescents (n  12), 2000 IU Vitamin D daily was associated
with an increase in serum vitamin D concentration, but
was not associated with consistent changes in body weight
(41). Similarly, a small, 8 week pilot study evaluating the
effect of daily supplementation at 2000 IU in 19 schizo-
phrenic adults treated with antipsychotics with low vita-
min D levels showed a significant improvement in vitamin
D level from baseline, but no change in anthropomorphic
or fasting metabolic parameters (42). The precise role of
low levels of vitamin D in the development of cardiometa-
bolic disease or in mental illness is unclear, and the evi-
dence supporting supplementation specifically in individ-
uals with mental illness is limited by the short duration of
treatment. However the strength of the association be-
tween metabolic risk and vitamin D level has provided an
impetus for evaluating levels and supplementing when
low. The current data suggest that low vitamin D levels
appear to enhance the impact of adiposity on hepatic fat
content. Further, when a general measure of inflamma-
tion, CRP, was introduced into the model, the interaction
between adiposity and vitamin D remained, suggesting a
possible different mechanism by which low vitamin D im-
pacts fat deposition in the liver. The results of our sensi-
tivity analysis for different cutoffs on high vs low Vitamin
D level (median split, 20 ng/mL or 30 ng/mL) suggest that
the strength of the relationship between DEXA fat and
liver fat increases as the vitamin D levels decrease. These
results warrant further research but they do support the
strategy proposed by others (20, 41) to supplement vita-
min D-deficient patients receiving antipsychotic drug
therapy.
This study is subject to important limitations. Specifi-
cally, sample size was relatively small and may have lead
to a failure to detect differences between groups on mea-
sures such as adiposity and CIMT. Further, there may be
uncontrolled confounding and bias (43). The antipsy-
chotic treated sample was heterogeneous, both in antipsy-
chotic treatment (eg, type of drug, dose, and length of
treatment) and in psychiatric diagnosis, as well as in treat-
ment with concurrent psychotropic medications like SS-
RIs and psychostimulants. Although stimulant medica-
tions may have an anorectic effect, they have not been
associated with significant weight loss in antipsychotic
treated individuals (44, 45). Therefore, including youth
who are treated with stimulants in studies of metabolic
effects associated with antipsychotic medications may in-
creasegeneralizabilityofresults,asconcomitantstimulant
use is common and representative of children commonly
treated with antipsychotic drug therapy in clinical settings
(25). In addition, Vitamin D needs may vary based on age
and stage of bone development, with potential effects on
measured Vitamin D levels (46). However, in this sample,
we found no effect of age on Vitamin D level. Future stud-
ies should carefully measure this. Finally, groups were not

matched on ethnicity, which may limit the interpretation
of results, particularly with respect to the relationship be-
tween adiposity and hepatic fat content, which may be
higher for lower adiposity in individuals of East Asian or
African Caribbean descent than in Caucasians (47). Fu-
ture analytic studies of larger sample size controlling for
age, ethnicity and concurrent psychotropic medications
are necessary and should provide important and relevant
data on the nature and time-course in the development of
cardiometabolic risk in children with and without anti-
psychotic drug treatment, including the possible roles of
low Vitamin D levels as well as whether there are benefits
of supplementation.
Despite these and perhaps other limitations, we believe
the most plausible interpretation of the data to be that
there are adverse effects of increasing adiposity on hepatic
fat content in children. These findings also support the use
of biomarkers to directly measure and accurately quantify
cardiometabolic risk in both antipsychotic treated and
nontreated children. While preliminary, the results of the
current study are compatible with various clinical propos-
als to monitor adiposity, and possibly Vitamin D level, in
children with high levels of adiposity to mitigate future
risk of cardiometabolic disease. Further research is needed
to test the hypothesis that low Vitamin D levels may be a
risk factor for increasing the adverse effect of adiposity on
risk for hepatic steatosis, both in antipsychotic treated
children as well as apparently healthy children with in-
creased adiposity.
